rpa1858.title: Real Property Act 1858 (South Australia), 21 Vict. No. 15 — An Act to simplify the Laws relating to the transfer and encumbrance of freehold and other interests in Land
rpa1858.author: Parliament of South Australia
rpa1858.quote: 31. No instrument shall be effectual to pass any estate or interest in any land under the operation of this Act, or to render such land liable as security for the payment of money, but so soon as the Registrar-General shall have entered the particulars thereof in the book of registry, and made endorsement on such instrument as hereinafter directed to be made in each such case respectively, the estate or interest shall pass or, as the case may be, the land shall become liable to security in manner and subject to the conditions and contingencies set forth and specified in such instrument
supports: Assent, as printed on the title page: "[Assented to, 27th January, 1858.]"
s 123, commencement: "This Act shall commence and take effect from and after the first day of July, one thousand eight hundred and fifty-eight."

s 31, simultaneous-presentation tie-break: "and should two or more instruments executed by the same proprietor, and purporting to transfer or encumber the same estate or interest in any land, be at the same time presented to the Registrar-General for registration and endorsement, he shall register and endorse that instrument, under which the person claims property, who shall present to him the grant or certificate of title of such land for that purpose."

s 33: "Every certificate of title or entry in the register book shall be conclusive, and vest the estate and interests in the land therein mentioned in such manner and to such effect as shall be expressed in such certificate or entry valid to all intents, save and except as is hereinafter provided in the case of fraud or error."

s 34, the assurance levy: "there shall be paid to the Registrar-General the sum of one farthing in the pound sterling on the value of the land so brought under the operation of this Act or so transmitted"

s 35: "All sums of money so received as aforesaid, shall be paid to the Treasurer of the said Province to constitute an Assurance Fund, out of which shall be made good the full amount awarded by any verdict or decree of Court to the rightful heir or proprietor of land under the operation of this Act as hereinafter provided, failing the recovery of such amount from the person who may by fraud, misrepresentation, or error, have become registered as proprietor of the same"

s 115, the map requirement: "It shall be lawful for the Registrar-General, if he shall think fit, to require the proprietor applying to have any land brought under the operation of this Act, or desiring to transfer or lease the same, or any portion thereof, to deposit, at the Registry Office, a map or plan of such land" ... "and is such proprietor shall neglect or refuse to comply with such requirement, it shall not be incumbent on the Registrar-General to proceed with the bringing of such land under the operation of this Act, or with the registration of such transfer or lease" (the "is" for "if" is in the printed transcript)
s 116: "Any person may, upon payment of a fee specified in Schedule T hereto, have access to the register book for the purpose of inspection"

Preamble: "WHEREAS the inhabitants of the Province of South Australia are subjected to losses, heavy costs, and much perplexity, by reason that the laws relating to the transfer and encumbrance of freehold and other interests in land are complex, cumbrous, and unsuited to the requirements of the said inhabitants"

s 91, the limit on indefeasibility as enacted: no action of ejectment lies against the registered proprietor "save and except only in the case of a mortgagee against his mortgagor ... or in case the registered proprietor has obtained such land by fraud or misrepresentation."

s 93, rollback by election where the wrong entry was error and not fraud: the person registered "through error or misconception, and not through fraud, misrepresentation, or deception" may, "in lieu of paying such sums of money so awarded as damages ... transfer such land to the person who shall have obtained such verdict"

s 94, rollback by order, and its limit: a court may direct cancellation where the registered proprietor was registered "through fraud or misrepresentation, or in any manner otherwise than as purchaser, or mortgagee for bona fide valuable consideration, or by transfer, or transmission from or through a purchaser or mortgagee for bona fide valuable consideration", whereupon the estate "shall thereupon revert to and vest in the persons in whom ... the same would have vested had no such entries been so made". The marginal note reads "But without prejudice to purchaser for bona fide valuable consideration." This is why the story says the register does not come back only once an innocent buyer has paid for it.

s 96, the Assurance Fund as backstop rather than first payer: damages are first levied by distress on the wrongdoer's goods, and only "in case of a return of nulla bona, or if the amount recovered by such distress shall not suffice" does the Registrar-General requisition the Treasurer to "charge the same to the account of the assurance fund"
s 102, the caveat's expiry: "Within three calendar months from the entering of such caveat, the person entering the same shall take proceedings to establish his claim"
rpa1858.note: Read as the full transcript PDF of the Act as enacted, hosted by the National Archives of Australia's Documenting a Democracy site; text extracted and read section by section. No type in the schema's enum covers a statute, so 'docs' is used. Sections 31-35, 91-98, 102, 114-116 and 123 were read in full from that transcript on 2026-08-22 by an independent checker.

low_griggs2014.title: Going through the obstruction, the Torrens System Assurance Fund and contemporary solutions - a tale weaved from a story of a nun, a romantic triangle and sibling corruption
low_griggs2014.author: Rouhshi Low and Lynden Griggs
low_griggs2014.quote: Compensation is payable when a person is deprived of land or an estate or interest in land.
supports: The purpose of the assurance fund today, quoted by the authors from Solak v Registrar of Titles (2011) 33 VR 40 at [88]: "The purpose of the fund is not to accumulate money but to provide compensation to persons who are deprived of an interest in land by the operation of the indefeasibility provisions."

Pedulla v Panetta (2011) 16 BPR 30,229, facts as summarised by the authors from [1]-[14] of the case: a forged power of attorney and forged authority put the plaintiff's brother on the register in 2007 for a consideration of $1; "In 2011, the brother and his partner finally sold the property to innocent purchasers for the sum of $3.8 million, settlement occurring in late April 2011"; "In May of 2011, the brother and his partner left Australia on separate flights and have not been seen since"; "Net proceeds to each of them were in excess of $684,000"; "On her return to Australia, Pedulla was penniless, distraught and without a home."
Costs: "Despite compensation in the sum of $3.8ml, which in the opinion of the authors was clearly available to the plaintiff, legal costs, which she also recovered, totalled over $329,000."

Every Australian jurisdiction still statutes a compensation scheme (authors' n 20): "Land Titles Act 1925 (ACT), s 143-151; Land Titles Act 1980 (Tas) ss 150-159; Land Title Act 2000 (NT), ss 192-196; Land Title Act 1994 (Qld), ss188-190; Real Property Act 1886 (SA) ss 201-205; Real Property Act 1900 (NSW) ss 128-135; Transfer of Land Act 1958 (Vic) ss 108-111; Transfer of Land Act 1893 (WA), s 201."

Torrens' own 1859 words on the fund, as quoted by the authors: "[The assurance fund] proceeds upon the principle of transferring the liability to claim by a rightful owner from the land itself to the person of the individual to whom certificate of title may be granted in error, the personal security being supplemented by an assurance fund"

Jurisdiction of the Pedulla compensation: the authors' nn 30-32 cite Pedulla v Panetta (No. 2) [2011] NSWSC 1533, and the defendant throughout is "the Registrar General" — New South Wales, under the Real Property Act 1900 (NSW) ss 128-135 of the authors' n 20. Not an inference from the BPR series alone.

adb1976.title: Torrens, Sir Robert Richard (1814-1884), Australian Dictionary of Biography, Volume 6
adb1976.author: Douglas J. Whalan
adb1976.quote: The basic principles of what was to become known outside South Australia as the Torrens system were: land titles no longer passed by the execution of deeds but by the registration of dealings on a public register; once registered the title of a purchaser became indefeasible unless he was guilty of fraud; and innocent dealers with interests in registered land were guaranteed either their interest in the land or monetary compensation therefor.
supports: "Torrens became collector of customs, probably through his father's influence as chairman of the colonization commission for South Australia; his salary was £350 (later £500)."
"He was appointed colonial treasurer and registrar-general in 1852"
"He stood for Adelaide in the House of Assembly elections of 1857 and, almost entirely because of his espousal of land titles reform, topped the poll."
"he published a further draft of his bill on 14 and 15 April and introduced it as a private member's bill in yet a third form on 4 June"
"Despite very strong opposition, mainly from the legal profession, it passed through both Houses and was assented to on 27 January 1858."
"Torrens resigned his seat in 1858 on becoming registrar-general under the Real Property Act at a salary of £1000."

"Torrens explained the system's operation in The South Australian System of Conveyancing by Registration of Title (1859); although he 'claimed authorship' of the system, it is clear that many people and influences helped considerably, including Ulrich Hübbe, Richard Bullock Andrews, George Fife Angas, Anthony Forster, William Burford, and, later, R. D. Hanson."

unverified: The opening deeds-conveyancing scenario — two buyers each searching the chain correctly and one still losing the land — is a generic characterisation of pre-register conveyancing, not a documented South Australian case. No source in this ledger asserts a specific double sale. The Act's own preamble supports only "losses, heavy costs, and much perplexity"; the prose keeps the scenario in the modal ("could") for that reason.

Ulrich Hübbe's and Anthony Forster's specific contributions to the drafting. ADB lists both among many who 'helped considerably' and notes Torrens 'claimed authorship'; the Hanseatic-origin thesis is contested in the literature and no primary source for it was opened. Neither man appears in the prose or on a card.

The commencement date. Several secondary pages give 2 July 1858; s 123 of the Act as printed reads 'from and after the first day of July, one thousand eight hundred and fifty-eight', and that is what the prose uses. The reason for the discrepancy was not established.

Torrens' 1859 pamphlet, The South Australian System of Conveyancing by Registration of Title, was not opened directly. Its 'going through the obstruction' passage is recorded here only as quoted by Low and Griggs, and is not used in the prose.
Frazer v Walker [1967] 1 AC 569 was not opened; no claim about indefeasibility beyond s 33's own words is made.

US title-insurance premium volume and the ALTA 'gap' endorsement. NAIC premium data and the ALTA policy forms were not opened, so no dollar figure or claim about American practice appears in the prose or on a card.

Whether a caveat under the 1858 Act could freeze a title indefinitely. s 102 gives the caveator three calendar months to take proceedings, which cuts against the 'lock with no expiry' framing, so that framing was dropped.

How far the 1858 Act's indefeasibility actually reached. s 33 makes an entry conclusive "save and except as is hereinafter provided in the case of fraud or error", and ss 91, 93 and 94 do permit ejectment, re-transfer and cancellation — but never against a purchaser for bona fide valuable consideration. The prose and cards now claim no more than that. Frazer v Walker [1967] 1 AC 569, which settled immediate indefeasibility a century later, was not opened.
